name: Composite streaming ASR+diar RTF on phone CPU (taskset C0, armed), accuracy byte-identical

description: Attacked the ~8.5 s/stream diar drain: (a) diar-only trailing silence before stream_finish (0/2/4 s) - no effect on the drain, transcript unchanged; (b) skipping stream_finish entirely - saves the whole 8.5 s but changes the transcript (finish also closes the turn still open at end-of-audio), so it is a diarisation change, not a free speedup. Metric unchanged: both flags default to off and stay in the tree as diagnostics.

asi.hypothesis: the 20 s of other_s is a fixed cost inside audiocpp_stream_finish and can be avoided
asi.mechanism_found: NOT overhead. libaudiocpp instrumentation shows the final flush emits ONE window and process_stream_windows spends 8.76 s on it; every window has encoder_frames=188, a FIXED-SIZE encoder pass. The diar costs ~8.5 s per ~26 s window; 'other_s' was simply the last window landing outside the per-piece timers. Short clips pay a whole window for 3 s of audio (7.27 s), which is exactly why it looked like a constant.
asi.probe_a: diar-only trailing silence 0/2/4 s -> drain 8.77/8.97/9.19 s (no effect). Side fact: 2-4 s of trailing silence leaves the transcript byte-identical.
asi.probe_b: skip stream_finish -> drain 0.00, single-pass RTF 0.7849->0.5922 (gate) and 0.7824->0.6578 (chat69), but transcript hash changes on both clips (15/23 blocks either way) - the final decode closes the turn still open at end-of-audio. Rejected under byte-identity.
asi.instrumentation_note: incremental rebuild of libaudiocpp.so for arm64 is 4 s, not the 27 min a full configure costs; ref/audiocpp is a git checkout at fc24c99 so instrument-and-revert is safe and cheap. The instrumented .so must be pushed back out of the device - measure.sh now hash-pushes it.
asi.real_lever: the loop is sequential: push diar (blocks on an 8.5 s window every ~26 s of audio) then accept asr. asr 49.7 s + diar 35.9 s per 228 s of audio, on 2 cores, with the two engines sharing nothing. Overlapping the legs is worth up to min(asr, diar) ~ 36 s per 228 s = RTF 0.47 -> ~0.28 ideal, vs 0.4651 now.
asi.next_action_hint: drive the diarizer from a worker thread fed by a (offset,len) queue into wav.pcm; main thread does asr_stream_accept only; join before the final attribute pass. Output must stay deterministic because speaker tagging happens in the FINAL attribute pass from the complete turn list - verify that assumption holds before trusting the byte-identity result.

description: Ran the diarizer on a worker thread so the two independent legs overlap instead of serialising (asr 49.7 s + diar 35.9 s per 228 s of audio). Rejected on the device: composite got 37-47% SLOWER. Metric reported as unchanged because the async path was reverted (commit daf62f7) and the shipped default path is the baseline tree.

asi.hypothesis: wall = asr + diar because the loop is sequential; overlapping the legs on the 2 A78s should approach max(asr, diar)
asi.result: strongly negative. Paired A/B in one armed window: gate_ms_v2 RTF 0.7848 -> 1.0743, chat69 0.7756 -> 1.1449. Both legs slowed about 2.8x (asr 24.87 -> 70.54 s, diar 20.26 -> 51.63 s) while total CPU work and peak RSS (412 MB) were unchanged.
asi.transcripts: byte-identical sync vs async (md5 db68a9da0e90 / 2929e3cfc15d) - the determinism argument held: tags come from the final attribute pass after joining the worker.
asi.mechanism_best_explanation: superlinear contention between two large streaming working sets (x-asr 168 MB + diar 106 MB) sharing the caches/DRAM bandwidth of the two A78s, plus 8 diar threads + 1 ASR thread on 2 cores. Not a spin-wait livelock, not the GPU path, not affinity (no --main-affinity was passed).
asi.ruling: sequential execution of the two legs is optimal on this device. Predicts any leg-concurrency variant loses; if a future change makes one leg much cheaper, re-test with the CHEAP leg overlapped rather than both.
asi.next_action_hint: structural win is elsewhere: the ASR leg reportedly runs on ONE thread (archive claim), i.e. 49.7 s of the 106 s wall occupies one core while the second core idles, and it cannot be hidden by overlap. Verify thread count on device (NEMO_DEBUG_THREADS prints it per piece) before attacking it.

description: Targeted retry of the leg-overlap dead end (#1082) with the assumption that caused the failure changed: the ASR leg at 1 thread (no 2-thread ggml barrier to spin on) and, in a second variant, each leg pinned to its own A78. asi.hypothesis: #1082's 2.8x loss came from a spinning 2-thread ggml barrier competing with diar threads; with ASR at 1 thread the overlap should pay off

asi.paired_chat69_rtf: A sync t=2 0.7773 (reference) | B sync t=1 1.1628 | C async t=1 0.8839 | D async t=1 + per-leg affinity 0.8831 | E async t=2 1.1291

asi.also_learned: thread scaling is real for both legs: ASR-only chat69 wall 34.83 s at t=1 vs 24.74 s at t=2; diar 31.45 s at t=1 vs 20.44 s at t=2. The -t flag sets BOTH legs' thread counts (bc.threads for audio.cpp, p.n_threads for CrispASR), so 'threads' is not an ASR-only knob today.

description: Prefault both models at init (charged to load_s, which is now printed) to test whether first-pass page faults inside the measured window cost anything. Net effect on the phone is zero: load grows by what wall shrinks. Metric is the unchanged baseline; the diagnostic and the load_s print stay in the tree.

asi.hypothesis: the measured window hides minor page faults on 274 MB of mmapped weights; touching them at init removes that cost
asi.result: it is a shift, not a win. Armed paired device runs: gate_ms_v2 wall 35.37 -> 35.24 s while load 0.20 -> 0.32 s (net +0.01 s); chat69 wall 53.96 -> 53.67 s with the same +0.12 s of load (net -0.17 s, inside noise).
asi.surprise: Engine::init is only 0.20 s on the phone - model load is essentially free (mmap + warm page cache). Any 'prefault the models' or 'first-window premium' theory is dead: there is no multi-second load cost to hide anywhere, unlike the 1.5B baseline's measured ~130 ms first-window premium.
asi.accounting_note: added load_s to [stats] precisely so this class of change cannot masquerade as a speedup: judge load_s + wall_s, never wall_s alone.

description: Removed the forced capacity padding in the diar streaming path (libaudiocpp): every window was being padded up to chunk_left_context+chunk_len+chunk_right_context and then packed up to spkcache_len+fifo_len+chunk_capacity, so the encoder paid full-capacity FLOPs even for a short drain window. Now the real lengths are used, the capacity checks remain as upper bounds, and the encoder already receives attention_mask(valid_frames, frames) so the padding was pure work. Byte-identical output (host gate hash, all three WERs, attribution and DER-lite unchanged) and composite 0.4227 -> 0.4177.

asi.change: ref/audiocpp commit 6f288b5: process_window_batch no longer resizes the feature buffer to chunk_left_context+chunk_len+chunk_right_context, and process_embedding_batch no longer forces packed_capacity to spkcache_len+fifo_len+chunk_capacity. The capacity checks stay as upper bounds. encode() already takes frames as a graph dimension and the encoder is handed attention_mask(valid_frames, frames), so the padding carried no information.
asi.why_this_matters: this was the mechanism behind the loop's unattributed 'other_s' (16 s of a 76 s protocol wall): the drain used to pay a full-capacity encoder pass for a couple of seconds of tail audio.
asi.why_only_1.2_pct: the padding saving is mostly eaten by graph REBUILD cost. ensure_encoder_graph re-plans the ggml graph whenever the frame count changes, so making the length dynamic means a new shape (and a new plan/arena) per window instead of one cached shape for the steady state. The tail is now nearly free, but we pay a rebuild on every window whose length differs from the last. That predicts the next move: bucket the dynamic length so consecutive windows reuse a cached graph.
asi.confidence: two rows at 0.4227 and 0.4177, both byte-identical to the same blessed hash (e7a4230a90d4 on device, 192184ebcd54977e host) and both armed (2297.5 / 2337.7 MHz). -1.2% is close to the noise floor, so this is kept as a strict no-regression simplification rather than a headline win; the 9.1% in #1088 is the real result.
asi.host_gate: byte-identical before the change and after: transcript hash 192184ebcd54977e unchanged, WER gate_ms_v2 0.1765 / holdout_en 0.2364 / holdout_zh 0.0791, attribution 0.0779 of 77, DER-lite 23.28%. No re-bless needed.

Add an NEMO_PROF timer around audiocpp_stream_finish and around the per-piece drain loop in engine.cpp and print the split, because this row falsified the assumption that other_s is a small padded tail: removing the tail padding left other_s at 16.1 s (was 16.4). Whatever it is, it is not tail padding.
asi.other_s_unchanged: 16.36 -> 16.11 s: the tail really was a small part of it.
asi.spkcache_robustness_check: while measuring this I mapped the spkcache_len cost curve to make sure #1088's 128 is not a fitted peak: outputs are byte-identical for 64/80/88/96/104/112/128 (same md5 on both protocol clips) and 160/264 are slower. Cost differences inside 64..128 are within run-to-run variance, so 128 stays as the mid-range choice; no change made.

description: Data-driven kernel pass #1 on the ASR leg: added an XASR_PROF eval-callback hook, measured the op mix on the phone, then removed the ggml_cont nodes that only feed elementwise consumers (5 sites + the attention score bias). Byte-identical, but zero measurable gain (0.4182 vs 0.4177) - which falsifies the naive reading of the profile: those small copies were not where the 22% CONT lives. Kept anyway as a strict simplification, plus the profiling hook, which is the durable artifact: the leg is only 31% MUL_MAT, so kernel work is aimed at data movement, not math.

asi.asr_op_mix_armed: XASR_PROF=1 (new eval-callback hook, observation only) on chat69, --no-diar: 615828 nodes accounted 29.8 s (profiling inflates the leg 15.4 -> 35.6 s and drops cores_used to 0.95, so treat the MIX as data and the absolute times as upper bounds): MUL_MAT 9.26 s 31.1% | ADD 6.57 s 22.1% | CONT 6.55 s 22.0% | UNARY 1.78 s 6.0% | MUL 1.36 s 4.6% | CONCAT 1.15 s 3.8% | IM2COL 0.93 s 3.1% | SSM_CONV 0.78 s 2.6% | PAD 0.44 s 1.5%. So HALF the ASR leg is data movement and elementwise work, not matmul.
asi.change: ref/crispasr e244691: rows_view() keeps the strided view for the five sites whose consumer is elementwise (NonlinAttention gate/value, conv chunk gate) and the attention score bias is added straight from its strided view. 8 fewer nodes per layer per step, same values, same accumulation order.
asi.falsified: removing those copies bought NOTHING measurable (asr_s 49.94 vs 49.83, rtf 0.4182 vs 0.4177). So the profiler's 22% CONT is NOT made of the small [hid, seq] slices - it must be the large attention permutes (Kh [qd,Tk,H], PE, Vt), the per-layer cache slices (out_tensor(last_cols(...))), and sheer node count. The lesson for the next attempt: the op MIX without call counts and byte counts is not actionable - a 22% slice can be 20 huge tensors or 200k tiny ones, and those need opposite fixes (fusion vs data movement).
asi.hook_kept: XASR_PROF=1 stays in the tree: it prints the per-op mix on xasr_free and is off unless the env var is set. Any further kernel work should start by extending it with calls + bytes per op, to tell 'few big copies' (fix the layout) from 'many tiny nodes' (fix the dispatch tax with fusion).
asi.next_two_candidate_targets: 1. Cache residency: every step writes 6 caches per layer (ck/cn/cv1/cv2/cc1/cc2) as out_tensor(last_cols(...)) and the host reads them back with get_output, then set_input copies them in again next step. That is graph->host->graph traffic that no amount of fusion removes; a ggml-native cache (llama.cpp-style, keep the tensors in the graph and double-buffer) would. Bit-identical, because the values never change - only who holds them. 2. Real fused kernels for the elementwise chain (bias_norm = sub/sqr/mean/sqrt/div/scale = 6 nodes, bypass = sub/mul/add = 3, swoosh = scale_bias/softplus/sub/scale_bias = 4), which is the ADD 22% + UNARY 6% + MUL 4.6% tax. asi.three_bugs_found_building_it: all silent rather than loud, all worth remembering: (1) GGUF array elements must NOT repeat the type field - the array header declares the element type once, and writing one per element desynchronised the entire KV block (the diar metadata has arrays of strings, so it failed immediately); (2) tensor offsets are relative to the DATA SECTION, so using the file size for the last tensor inflates it by the header length, and because b'\0' * negative is a no-op rather than an error, every subsequent tensor lands early while the file still parses; (3) a metadata helper that returns a DEFAULT on a miss turns 'wrong namespace' into 'corrupt model' - the first bundle attempt loaded the weights fine and failed with 'inconsistent hyper-parameters' because vocab_size resolved to 0, since only the tensor lookup had been made prefix-aware. description: The biggest win of the session, found by instrumentation rather than theory. asi.mechanism: MelFilterbank::compute_custom walked all 128 mels x 257 frequency bins for every frame and accumulated in long double, which on ARM64 is software-emulated IEEE quad precision (__multf3/__addtf3 calls, not FPU ops). The diarizer's own filterbank has 504 nonzero weights out of 32,896 - 1.5%, 2.0 bins per mel - so 98.5% of that arithmetic was multiplying and adding exact zeros. Visiting only the nonzero weights, in the same ascending-frequency order, is bit-identical: adding +0 to a finite partial sum is exact, and the only possible divergence is a sum of exactly zero, where -0.0 and +0.0 both feed the same log(x + 2^-24). The dense path is retained for genuinely dense banks so no other model is pessimised.

Storing it as f16 and widening each group to f32 before a single-accumulator FMA takes the phase to 1.11 s, and the whole ASR leg to 38.59 s. This row also fixes a harness bug that had been producing fake numbers: both build scripts piped cmake to /dev/null without checking the exit status, so a compile error in a dependency was swallowed and the stale archive was measured as if it were the change.

asi.bigger_than_the_microbenchmark_suggested: the joint phase itself went 3.87 -> 1.11 s, i.e. -2.76 s per 69 s clip, but the protocol's asr_s fell by 9.1 s over 4 runs (-19%) and cores_used rose 1.70 -> 1.81. More than the joint's own saving: the joint had been streaming 10.2 MB per encoder frame, and that traffic was starving every other phase sharing the two cores. This is the same lesson as the elementwise findings, in the opposite direction - on this device, work that is NOT on the critical path still moves the wall clock when it consumes shared bandwidth. p95 piece 97.1 -> 79.1 ms and first partial 0.306 -> 0.263 s came along with it.
asi.harness_bug_this_row_fixed: the most important thing in this row is not the number. scripts/build_android.sh and scripts/build_host.sh piped `cmake --build` to /dev/null WITHOUT checking the exit status, so a compile error in a dependency was swallowed and the previous archive got linked, pushed, measured and reported as if it were the change. That produced two confident, completely meaningless results earlier in this session (the first f16 attempt, and the NEON four-accumulator experiment that 'proved' vectorising does not help). Both scripts now fail loudly and print the compiler's errors before anything can be measured. If you change a dependency and the timing does not move AT ALL, suspect this class of bug before believing the physics.
asi.hypothesis: the transducer joint is bandwidth-bound on its 10.2 MB matrix, so halving the bytes should cut the phase

asi.mechanism: the joint is a [5000 x 512] matvec per encoder frame in plain host C++ - 4.4 GMAC and 10.2 MB of weight reads per 69 s clip, 3.87 s measured, 31% of the ASR leg, and completely invisible to the ggml eval-callback profile because it is not a ggml op. The session moved the composite from 0.4651 to 0.2692 by removing work that was never model work at all: a filterbank multiplying 98.5% zeros in software quad precision, a 4,000-node graph rebuilt every step, and a 10.2 MB matvec streamed once per encoder frame.

description: Ported the two bit-identical ggml CPU fixes (per-element 64-bit division in the non-contiguous binary-op index; unconditional two-thread split of small copy/elementwise ops) into audiocpp's vendored ggml, on the hypothesis that the diar encoder would feel them where the matmul-bound ASR leg did not - its graph is elementwise-heavy (285 ADD nodes over 76M elements and 312 MUL over 41M per window, against 128 MUL_MAT). Byte-identical on the gate as expected, and measurably flat: 0.2695 vs 0.2692, diar_s 15.01 vs 14.94. That closes the class properly - the same fixes measured 0% on the ASR leg and now 0% on the diar leg - so the remaining composite time is matmul arithmetic and weight streaming in kernels we do not own, not elementwise dispatch.

asi.closes_a_class: this is the same pair of fixes, in the other ggml, landing on a different cost structure - and measuring 0.0% again. Combined with the crispasr results (#1091, #1092), the conclusion is now properly bounded rather than assumed: on this composite, neither copy of ggml spends meaningful time in the non-contiguous elementwise path or in per-op thread dispatch, on either leg. The elementwise tax is real in the source and free in practice, because it is hidden under matmuls and memory streaming.
asi.fixed_while_proving_it_irrelevant: the changes stay: they remove a 64-bit division per element and a barrier per small op, in a path that other configurations (bigger tensors, more threads, a machine with more cores) would feel. They are bit-identical and strictly less work. Keeping a fix that measures 0% is fine when the fix is unambiguously a reduction in work; keeping it because it might help later is not a reason, and this row is the evidence that it does not help now.
asi.hypothesis: audiocpp's vendored ggml is a different copy from the one already fixed, and the diar encoder is elementwise-heavy (285 ADD nodes/76M elements and 312 MUL/41M per window vs only 128 MUL_MAT), so the same two bit-identical fixes should land there even though they measured 0% on the matmul-bound ASR leg
asi.measurement: armed, witness 2314.6 MHz / 93.5% at 2.4 GHz, battery 355. phone_rtf 0.2695 vs 0.2692, diar_s 15.01 vs 14.94, other_s 7.71 vs 7.76, asr_s 38.71 vs 38.67 - all inside the 0.05% run-to-run spread, i.e. no effect. Byte-identical on the gate (hash 192184ebcd54977e) and checks passed.
asi.what_the_composite_is_now_made_of: ASR ~63% (encoder matmuls on int8 SDOT, plus a 1.11 s f16 joint), diar ~24% (its transformer encoder), drain ~13% (one final window, and the price of bounded turn latency). Both encoders' weight formats are insensitive because every quantised ggml type declares vec_dot_type = Q8_0, so activations are quantised and dotted with SDOT whatever the weights are. What is left is arithmetic and weight streaming in kernels we do not own: KleidiAI (needs a network fetch) or a different model (outside the contract).
asi.also_checked_and_closed: x-asr's left context: the implementation reads xasr.left_context_frames = [96, 256, 256, 256] as a table INDEXED BY chunk_ms (160 -> 96, 480 -> 256), not per encoder stage, and then divides the chosen value by each stage's downsampling factor. So the shipped 256 is the model's own geometry for the shipped 480 ms chunk, not an implementation over-provision - a hypothesis raised and dropped in one read rather than by experiment.

description: Pinned the dependency worktrees and made the build refuse to run against anything else. Every optimisation of this session lives in ref/crispasr and ref/audiocpp - two separate repositories outside this project, which tracked only a patch file - so a clean checkout would have rebuilt the 0.47 baseline while the ledger claimed 0.269, with nothing to say so. deps.lock now records the three heads with a note on what each contains, and scripts/check_deps.sh (called by both build scripts) fails on drift or a dirty worktree unless ALLOW_DEPS_DRIFT=1. This is the swallowed-cmake-exit-code lesson one level up: a dependency that is not what you think it is is indistinguishable from an optimisation that did not work. Metric unchanged at 0.2691, as expected for a row that changes no measured code.

asi.measurement: armed, witness 2043.6 MHz but only 78.0% of time at the 2.4 GHz step - a weaker arm than the last three rows (92.6-93.5%) - and the result is still 0.2691, matching 0.2692/0.2693/0.2695. A useful accidental robustness check: the composite now reproduces within 0.15% across a 10-point swing in the 2.4 GHz residency share, whereas earlier in the session the same protocol moved 10% on a comparable swing. The per-leg split is unchanged too (asr 38.64, diar 14.94, other 7.76).
asi.no_metric_change_this_row: phone_rtf 0.2691 vs 0.2692: nothing in the measured path moved, and that is the point of the row. The work was making the measurement trustworthy, not making the code faster.
asi.the_general_lesson_is_the_whole_session_: Three separate times this session, a measurement said something false and the code was innocent: cmake exit codes swallowed so a stale archive was measured as a fresh one (twice), and a dependency worktree that nothing tracked so a clean checkout would have rebuilt the 0.47 baseline while the ledger claimed 0.269. Each was found by disbelieving a number, and each is now structurally prevented rather than documented: the build fails loudly on a compile error, and it refuses to build against unpinned dependencies. The optimisations themselves were found by disbelieving a label - three separate 'model-bound' legs were carrying signal processing, bookkeeping and host matvecs that no model profiler could see.
asi.verification_done: (1) deps.lock matches all three worktrees and a full host rebuild reproduces the blessed transcript hash 192184ebcd54977e. (2) Negative test: moving audiocpp's git HEAD makes check_deps.sh exit 1 and build_host.sh exit 1 with the message 'the result will not correspond to the recorded numbers'; restoring it returns both to 0. A guard that has never been seen to fail is a guard that does not work, so it was tested against a deliberately broken state rather than assumed. (3) crispasr's gitlink for its ggml submodule now names the measured commit, so crispasr is clean and a checkout there can no longer revert the CPU fixes.
asi.whats_left: unchanged and honestly bounded: both encoders are on int8 SDOT and weight-format-insensitive by construction (every quantised ggml type declares vec_dot_type = Q8_0), the elementwise path is measured irrelevant on both legs, the joint is f16 and down to 1.11 s, the drain is one final window and the price of bounded turn latency, and the merged single-GGUF deployment is in place and neutral. The only remaining levers are KleidiAI (blocked on a network fetch for the arm_llama kernels), a one-runtime merge whose ceiling has shrunk as core utilisation rose from 1.61/2 to 1.81/2, and a cheaper model pair (outside the contract).

description: Tested the one remaining geometry lever in the ASR encoder: the model's left_context_frames table is indexed by chunk_ms ([160,480,960,1920] -> [96,256,256,256]), so the shipped 480 ms chunk carries 256 frames of left context where the model's own 160 ms chunk carries 96, and per-stage attention is O(seq x (left/ds + seq)). Added a measurement hook (XASR_LEFT_CTX, inert by default) and probed 192/128/96 on the host: the speed available is 2-5% of the ASR leg and the cost is severe and non-monotonic - gate_ms_v2 WER 0.1765 -> 0.2000 / 0.3059 / 0.2471. Rejected on accuracy, no re-bless, default unchanged and gate byte-identical. The useful by-product is that attention is only ~5% of the encoder, so its cost is dominated by left-context-independent FFN/conv matmuls.

asi.cost_of_closing_it_was_one_commit: the whole question cost one committed hook and two host runs, because the hypothesis was cheap to test in the shape the model actually ships it: a table indexed by chunk_ms, readable in one grep. That is the third time this session that reading the model's own metadata answered a question that would otherwise have become an experiment - the other two being the supported chunk_ms set [160, 480, 960, 1920] and the weight dtypes (298 q5_0, 619 f32, 49 f16 in a file named q8_0).
asi.encoder_cost_structure_now_measured: this is the useful by-product: per-stage attention is only ~5% of the encoder (a 2.7x cut in left context bought 5% of the ASR leg on the host, and less than that after the 2-5% that the non-attention part of the graph accounts for). So the ASR encoder's cost is dominated by work that is INDEPENDENT of left context - the FFN and conv blocks and their matmuls - which is consistent with everything else: weight-format insensitivity, SDOT-bound matmuls, elementwise fixes worth 0%. There is no geometry that makes this encoder cheaper; only fewer FLOPs or faster kernels.
asi.hypothesis: the model's left_context_frames table is indexed by chunk_ms, pairing 480 ms with 256 frames of context where 160 ms gets 96; since per-stage attention is O(seq x (left/ds + seq)), the shipped pairing may be leaving a large compute reduction on the table
asi.measurement: armed, witness 2306.4 MHz / 93.0% at 2.4 GHz, battery 355. phone_rtf 0.2684 (vs 0.2691), asr_s 38.50 (vs 38.64), all inside the 0.05% spread: the shipped default is unchanged, as intended, since the hook is inert unless XASR_LEFT_CTX is set. Gate byte-identical (hash 192184ebcd54977e), checks passed.
asi.not_overfitting_because_it_failed: worth being explicit: a 3% speed gain for +13 WER points on the primary gate clip is not a trade worth making on any reading, and the 96 case (+7 points for 5%) is the same story softer. Nothing here was tuned against the benchmark - the values probed are the model's own declared left contexts, and the direction of the result (smaller context is much worse) is a property of the model, not of these clips.
asi.next: The encoder's remaining cost is left-context-independent arithmetic in kernels we do not own: KleidiAI (network-blocked), a one-runtime merge whose ceiling keeps shrinking as utilisation rises, or a different model (outside contract). The one host-side item left is the ASR cache round-trip (outputs 0.56 + inputs 0.20 s per 69 s clip, 114 cache tensors per step going graph -> host vector -> graph); it is bit-identical in principle, but every host-side phase measured so far has been hidden under the matmuls, so it should be expected to be worth ~1% and not more.
asi.rejected_on_accuracy_host_evidence: gate_ms_v2 WER by left context: 256 (shipped) 0.1765 in 4.11 s | 192 -> 0.2000 (+2.4 pts, -2% time) | 128 -> 0.3059 (+12.9 pts, -3% time) | 96 -> 0.2471 (+7.1 pts, -5% time). The speed available is 2-5% of the ASR leg; the accuracy cost is an order of magnitude larger than anything the re-bless policy would accept, and the non-monotonicity (96 better than 128) says the decoder is sensitive to where the context boundary lands, not merely to its size. The model's pairing of 256 with a 480 ms chunk is load-bearing.
asi.tooling_note_the_guard_fired_on_me: the new deps guard immediately caught this iteration's first attempt: I edited crispasr and ran a build without committing, so check_deps.sh refused and the probe silently ran the PREVIOUS binary - two identical rows (4.02/4.03 s, identical WER) that would have read as 'the override does nothing'. Committing the dependency first, then measuring, is now the enforced workflow. That is the second time this session a stale binary nearly produced a confident wrong conclusion.

description: Attacked the last identified host-side item in the ASR leg: the per-step cache round-trip was allocating 114 fresh vectors per step (~16.5k per 69 s clip), most above glibc's 128 KB mmap threshold and therefore mmap/munmap pairs with page faults and TLB churn on top of the memcpy. Reading into reused buffers is bit-identical (host gate unchanged) and measurably flat: 0.2693 vs 0.2684, asr_s 38.65 vs 38.50. That is the fourth consecutive 0% for host-side ASR work, and it sharpens the rule: the per-step graph rebuild DID pay because it serialises before a compute, while work between computes overlaps with the matmuls on the other core.

asi.change: crispasr d879f4b: get_output_into() reads the 114 per-step cache tensors and the encoder output into REUSED buffers. kv.second = get_output(...) returned a fresh vector every step, so the previous buffer was freed and a new one allocated 16.5k times per 69 s clip, most of them above glibc's 128 KB mmap threshold and therefore mmap/munmap pairs with page faults and TLB churn. Bit-identical by construction (same tensor, same bytes, same values) and the host gate confirms it.
asi.hypothesis: the ASR cache round-trip costs more than its bytes because every step allocates 114 fresh vectors, most above glibc's mmap threshold, so the copies carry page-fault and TLB churn on top of the memcpy
asi.measurement: armed, witness 2311.4 MHz / 93.3% at 2.4 GHz, battery 356. phone_rtf 0.2693 vs 0.2684/0.2691/0.2692/0.2695 across the last rows - inside the 0.05% spread, i.e. no effect. asr_s 38.65 vs 38.50, diar_s and other_s unchanged. Gate byte-identical (hash 192184ebcd54977e), checks passed.
asi.process_wart_found_and_fixed: the deps guard caught a workflow bug of my own making: last iteration's row ended in 'discard', which reverts UNCOMMITTED changes in this repo - and my deps.lock update for that iteration's dependency commit was uncommitted, so the lock silently rolled back to an older head and the next build refused to run. The lock update is now committed as part of the experiment, not left beside it. Worth knowing for anyone extending this harness: anything that must survive a discard has to be committed before the row, not after.
asi.the_distinction_this_row_sharpens: four host-side ASR changes have now measured 0%: copy removal (#1091), thread-partition threshold and index arithmetic (#1092), and now buffer reuse. But one host-side change DID pay: building the 4,000-node graph per step (#1098, ~0.55 s/clip). The difference is where the work sits relative to a compute: work that must FINISH before the next compute can start is on the critical path and cannot be hidden, while work between computes overlaps with the matmuls on the other core. So 'host-side' is not the discriminator - 'serialised before a compute' is. That is a sharper rule than 'host work is hidden' and it is what should guide any future attempt on this leg.
asi.what_remains_and_why_it_is_all_external: with host-side work bounded, geometry bounded (left context and chunk_ms both rejected on accuracy with the model's declared values), weight format bounded (every quantised ggml type declares vec_dot_type = Q8_0, so the dot is int8 SDOT whatever the weights are) and the frontend bounded (18x already), what remains in the 61 s protocol wall is (a) encoder matmul arithmetic in kernels we do not own - KleidiAI, blocked on a network fetch for the arm_llama kernels; (b) the one-runtime merge, whose ceiling has shrunk as utilisation rose from 1.61/2 to 1.81/2; (c) a cheaper model pair, outside the contract; (d) the ggml-native cache round-trip, which is the one remaining host-side item with a real mechanism, but this row is direct evidence that it will be worth ~0% because it sits between computes rather than before one.

description: Tested whether the diar encoder's 6.6 s/clip could reach the A78's fp16 FMLA by converting its q5_0 weights to f16 - a live idea, since audiocpp's ggml (unlike CrispASR's patched copy) has F16 wired to the native vec_dot_f16. Refuted by arithmetic before writing the converter: every quantised ggml type already declares vec_dot_type = Q8_0, so both models run int8 SDOT, which on Cortex-A78 is ~4x the fp32 FMA rate while fp16 FMLA is ~2x. The models are already on the fastest arithmetic the core has, so f16 would move the encoder DOWN a rung. Recorded in the design note and backlog so the lever is closed by mechanism rather than by five failed requantisation experiments. Metric unchanged at 0.2684, gate byte-identical.

asi.arithmetic_ranking_on_this_core: per cycle on Cortex-A78 (ARMv8.2-A, two 128-bit NEON pipes): SDOT int8 ~4x the fp32 FMA rate, fp16 FMLA ~2x, fp32 1x. Both models are on the 4x path already, so the fastest arithmetic this core has is in use and there is no precision move left that does not go DOWN the ladder.
asi.hypothesis: the diar encoder spends 6.6 s per 69 s clip in transformer matmuls, and audiocpp's ggml - unlike CrispASR's patched copy - has F16 wired to the native vec_dot_f16, so f16 weights might reach the A78's fp16 FMLA and beat the current q5_0 path
asi.measurement: armed, witness 2307.6 MHz / 93.1% at 2.4 GHz, battery 361. phone_rtf 0.2684, asr_s 38.52, diar_s 14.90, other_s 7.77 - unchanged tree, gate byte-identical (hash 192184ebcd54977e), checks passed.
asi.one_grep_prevented_an_hour: the whole question was decided before writing a q5_0 dequantiser: audiocpp's type table really does have F16 -> vec_dot_f16 (no CrispASR-style patch), so the idea was live, and it was the core's arithmetic that killed it rather than any assumption about ggml. Reading the two tables first is the cheap half of this session's method; the expensive half is only worth spending once the answer is not already sitting in a header.
asi.state_of_the_loop: five consecutive rows now sit at 0.2684-0.2695, a 0.4% band, with every lever class closed by a mechanism rather than a null result: geometry (left context, chunk_ms, diar chunk/fifo) by the model's own declared values being load-bearing; weight format by the int8/fp16/fp32 ranking; host-side ASR work by 'serialised before a compute' vs 'between computes'; the frontend by an 18x fix already banked; and the deployment layer by a merged single GGUF that is neutral by design. What remains is external (KleidiAI needs a network fetch) or outside the contract (a cheaper model pair, a one-runtime merge whose ceiling has shrunk to 1.81/2 cores).
asi.what_this_row_changes_for_the_record: nothing measured - the value is that the model-format lever is now closed by arithmetic rather than by five failed experiments. Anyone who later proposes 'try f16 weights' or 'try q4 because it is smaller' can be answered with the type table and the core's instruction throughput instead of re-running the sweep.

description: Fixed .auto/validate.sh --compare, which had been failing quietly since I wrote it: it looked for a token count in a field the scorer does not print, the parse raised, the except branch swallowed it, and every clip came back as '(missing)' - so two comparisons this session had to be redone by hand. Rewritten around what the scorer actually emits, reporting per clip the recomputed WER and delta, whether the text is identical once labels and segment joins are removed, how many speaker labels churned, and the word-level edit distance; plus a micro-average from S/D/I/H and a sign test that discards ties (the old formula counted ties in n and printed p=0.001 for a result where nothing moved). Validated against a case whose answer is known independently: ref vs the f16-joint candidate gives all 11 clips WER-equal, micro 0.1019 with identical counts, text identical on 8 of 11, and the 3 differing being precisely the English clips with a boundary space. Also declined to implement the largest remaining structural idea after reading that it is chunk_ms=960's encoder geometry - already measured and rejected on accuracy.

asi.lever_i_considered_and_rejected_before_i: the largest remaining structural idea was batching several chunks per graph execution, which would halve the encoder's weight traffic (23 GB per 69 s clip) and cut the overlap recomputation. It was NOT implemented, because it is chunk_ms=960's encoder geometry with a different decoder cadence, and chunk_ms=960 was already measured and rejected (+5.9 WER on gate_ms_v2, past the holdout_en ceiling). Spending an hour to re-derive a closed result is how sessions waste their last hours; reading the earlier row was cheaper and just as informative.
asi.measurement: armed, witness 2307.7 MHz / 93.0% at 2.4 GHz, battery 361. phone_rtf 0.2683, asr_s 38.49, diar_s 14.95, other_s 7.72 - unchanged tree, gate byte-identical (hash 192184ebcd54977e), checks passed. Six consecutive rows now sit in 0.2683-0.2695.
asi.same_failure_mode_as_the_build_scripts: this is the third instance of one pattern, which is worth naming as a class: a tool that fails QUIETLY and looks like it worked. cmake exit codes swallowed (twice, producing fake measurements), a GGUF writer that parsed but misplaced data by exactly one header length, a deps lock that a discard silently rolled back, and now a comparison that reported '(missing)' for every clip while exiting 0. Each was found by checking whether the output was plausible rather than by reading it - '(missing)' on eleven clips is implausible, and so was a 0.0% result from a build that had not compiled. The general rule for this repo: every tool that reports a result should be able to report FAILURE loudly, and a surprising number should be treated as a bug until proven otherwise.
asi.the_general_lesson_is_the_whole_session_: Three separate times this session, a measurement said something false and the code was innocent: cmake exit codes swallowed so a stale archive was measured as a fresh one (twice), and a dependency worktree that nothing tracked so a clean checkout would have rebuilt the 0.47 baseline while the ledger claimed 0.269. Each was found by disbelieving a number, and each is now structurally prevented rather than documented: the build fails loudly on a compile error, it refuses to build against unpinned dependencies, and the accuracy comparison now reports its own parse failures instead of swallowing them. The optimisations themselves were found by disbelieving a label - three separate 'model-bound' legs were carrying signal processing, bookkeeping and host matvecs that no model profiler could see.

description: Added per-window encode timing to the diarizer and used it to test three explanations for an anomaly I had spotted, all of which turned out to be wrong in instructive ways: (1) cross-engine thread contention - the 2x middle window survives with --no-asr, so it is internal to the diarizer; (2) ggml worker spin - poll=50 is only ~4 ms of spinning, which cannot explain 1.8 s becoming 3.6 s, so the hypothesis died on arithmetic before I built the override; (3) first-touch page faults - faults are front-loaded into window 1 (49.5k) yet that window is the CHEAPEST per frame, so faults are not the driver. The real finding required measuring the denominator: per-window frames are 380/548/351 and the cost is linear at 4.85/5.46/4.89 ms per frame. That closes the 'something hidden in the diar encoder' question and turns the one remaining structural idea - caching the carried speaker state's per-layer K/V, which the causal attention mask makes mathematically valid - into a sized estimate of ~2.2 s per 69 s clip, about 7% of the composite. Metric unchanged at 0.2659, gate byte-identical.

asi.correction_i_made_mid_iteration: my first reading of the per-window times was wrong and the instrumentation corrected it: I concluded cost was 'anti-correlated with window size' from two numbers whose window sizes I had estimated by hand. Measuring the sizes showed 380 / 548 / 351 frames, and the cost is linear in them (4.85 / 5.46 / 4.89 ms per frame). The middle window of chat69 is not anomalous at all - it is simply the largest window, because by then the speaker cache is full and the chunk plus state reaches 548 frames. The rule that earned its keep this session is 'measure the denominator too': a per-item time is meaningless without the item size.
asi.diagnostic_value_the_bounty_is_now_sized: the linear cost model turns the one remaining structural idea into a number instead of a maybe. The diar encoder processes (speaker cache 128 + fifo 40 + chunk) frames per window and re-encodes the 168 state frames every time; the attention mask is CAUSAL (keys at or beyond lengths are masked to -10000), so those state frames' per-layer K/V are mathematically identical to what the previous window computed and could be carried in a cache. At a measured 4.9-5.5 ms per frame, dropping 168 of every ~508 frames is ~33% of the encoder: roughly 2.2 s per 69 s clip, about 7% of the composite, and bit-identical in principle. That is a real project - expose 12 layers x K/V as graph outputs, ring-buffer them alongside the existing speaker cache, and process only the chunk frames - and it is now the best-evidenced thing left in contract.
asi.falsified_hypotheses_this_iteration: 1. 'The other engine's threads are stealing the diar encoder's time.' The 2x middle window survives with --no-asr (diar-only: 1.832 / 3.147 / 1.703), so it is internal to the diarizer, not cross-engine contention. 2. 'ggml's worker spin is stealing cores.' poll defaults to 50, i.e. n_rounds = 131072 x 50 ~ 6.5M pause iterations, which is about 4 ms of spinning - nowhere near enough to turn a 1.8 s window into 3.6 s. The arithmetic killed it before I built the env override. 3. 'The expensive window is paying first-touch page faults.' Faults ARE front-loaded (49.5k in window 1, then 16.3k, 10.0k) but window 1 is the CHEAPEST per frame (4.85 ms), so faults are not what makes a window expensive; they are the cost of paging in ~198 MB of weights once, and prefaulting would only move it out of the measured window.

description: CORRECTION of the previous row. It recorded a ~7% opportunity - caching the diar encoder's carried speaker-state K/V across windows - because the attention mask was described as causal. Re-reading the code before building it, that is wrong: the mask is [batch, 1, frames, frames] and masks only keys at or past the VALID LENGTH, with no position-dependent mask anywhere (build_encoder_layer passes that tensor to the attention module and nothing else). Attention over [speaker cache | fifo | chunk] is therefore bidirectional, as Sortformer-with-AOS intends. That inverts the conclusion: each state frame's representation depends on the newest chunk frames, so carrying its K/V forward would quietly convert bidirectional chunk attention into causal attention and change the output. The state frames are irreducibly recomputed, and the ~2.2 s/clip estimate is void. Correction recorded in the design note, the backlog and this row. Metric unchanged at 0.2659, gate byte-identical.

asi.how_the_error_happened: I wrote 'the mask is causal' in the previous row's ASI after skimming a loop that indexes `key` from `lengths[batch]` to `frames` and masks those entries. What I should have asked, and did not, is what the loop does NOT mask: within [0, lengths) every query still sees every key. Reading for the presence of a mask is not the same as reading what the mask permits - and a mask's SHAPE ([batch, 1, frames, frames], one mask for all query positions) was the tell that it could not be positional, since a causal mask necessarily varies by query.

asi.rule_worth_keeping: before building any cache on top of an attention mask, check whether the mask is indexed by POSITION or only by VALIDITY. A validity mask says 'ignore the padding'; a causal mask says 'ignore the future'. They look nearly identical in code, they mean opposite things, and only one of them makes incremental decoding legal at all. A mask that is the same tensor for every query position cannot be causal - that is a one-line check that would have caught this before it reached the ledger.
asi.scope_of_the_correction: the correction is recorded in three places so it cannot be inherited silently: the design note gains a section stating that the state cannot be cached and why; the backlog entry that promised ~7% is replaced with the negative result; and the earlier row's claim is named as wrong rather than quietly overwritten. An earlier iteration in this session already had to revert a diar geometry change for moving speaker decisions - the habit of correcting the record in place, rather than editing history, is the reason those reversals were caught at all.
asi.the_opportunity_does_not_exist: the carried 168-frame speaker state is ~33% of every window's packed length (spkcache 128 + fifo 40 + chunk), and with the encoder measured linear at 4.85-5.46 ms per frame that looked like ~2.2 s per 69 s clip, about 7% of the composite. It is not available. Because attention is bidirectional over the packed region, every state frame's representation is a function of the newest chunk frames as well as its own history; carrying its K/V forward would freeze it against the current window's audio. The state frames are irreducibly recomputed, and the only remaining way to shrink that term is a smaller spkcache_len - which changes which frames get assigned to which speaker, and has already been taken from 264 to 128 on re-blessed evidence.
asi.what_is_left_is_now_all_external_or_out_: with the last in-contract structural idea closed by inspection rather than by measurement, the composite's remaining time is: encoder arithmetic in int8 SDOT on both legs (KleidiAI is the only kernel lever and is verified network-blocked - both ggml copies ship the glue, no ai_micro_kernels exists on this machine), a drain that is one final window and the price of bounded turn latency, and host-side work that has measured 0% four times because it sits between computes. The honest summary is that this session moved the composite 0.4651 -> 0.2659 (-42.8%) entirely by removing work that was never model work, and what remains is work that is.

description: Closed a contract gap in the validation tool and used the repaired tool to produce cumulative accuracy evidence. The session's rule is that first-output latency must not get worse, but nothing checked it: checks.sh verifies bytes and WER, and the protocol times two clips. The f16 joint is exactly the change that could flip an early argmax, so it was the one most in need of a check that did not exist; every validation clip now reports first-partial and p95-piece with bounds. Separately, --compare was scoring ZERO clips and printing an empty table - which reads as 'no difference', the most dangerous way for this tool to fail - because each run truncated the index that held other tags' manifest mappings; the index is now gone and manifests are derived. With that fixed, ref (captured before this session's mel filterbank, padding, graph-reuse and f16 changes) versus the current build is WER-identical on all 11 clips with micro 0.1019 and identical S/D/I/H. Metric unchanged at 0.2671.

asi.cumulative_accuracy_effect_is_zero: the repaired comparison gives the strongest accuracy statement of the session, and it is cumulative rather than per-change: ref was captured BEFORE the mel filterbank fix, the window-padding removal, the graph-reuse/UAF fix, the f16 joint, the buffer reuse and the audiocpp ggml CPU fixes. Against the current build, all 11 clips are WER-identical, the micro-average is 0.1019 with identical S/D/I/H (245/69/11/2865), text is identical on 8 of 11 and differs only by a segment-boundary space on the 3 English clips, and the sign test is vacuous. Every kept change together move no words on ~1720 s of two languages.
asi.empty_table_is_the_dangerous_failure: a comparison that scores zero clips and prints an empty table is indistinguishable, at a glance, from a comparison that found no differences - and that second reading is the one a reader wants. The cause was mundane and invisible: every run truncated index.tsv, deleting the other tags' manifest mappings. The fix removes the file rather than repairing it, because the clip-to-manifest mapping is derivable from the clip name and a derived fact cannot go stale; a clip that exists but cannot be scored now prints UNSCORED rather than being skipped, for the same reason. This is the fourth tool in this repo to fail quietly, and the second time the pattern was 'a table that looks like a result'.
asi.latency_contract_previously_unverified: the session's rules say first-output latency must not get worse, and until now nothing checked it: checks.sh verifies bytes and WER, and the protocol only times two clips. The f16 joint is precisely the change that could flip an early argmax and move first output, so it was the change most in need of a check that did not exist. Each validation clip now reports first-partial and p95-piece from the run's own [stats] line, with bounds (1.0 s / 150 ms) that can be overridden. Across all 11 clips the shipped build reports 0.13-0.27 s and ~41 ms on the host with no warnings, and the protocol's device numbers are 0.252 s and 77.7 ms - both better than the 0.32 s / 101 ms the session started from.

description: Wrote docs/kernel-brief.md - the specification for the only lever still open, built from this session's measurements rather than from the model files. It quantifies the target: both encoders already run on the fastest arithmetic the A78 has (int8 SDOT via every quantised type's vec_dot_q8_0) and achieve only 13-20% of it - ~12.7 G MAC/s effective for x-asr (12.4 M useful MACs per emitted frame, with a 61-row window emitting 12 frames, so real work is ~5x that) and ~20 G MAC/s for the diar. It names three mechanisms in order of value, and deliberately puts the bit-identical one first: ggml re-quantises activations on every mul_mat call while a block feeds the same tensor to three or four matmuls, so quantising once per tensor per step is free and needs no new kernel. It states the ceiling (25-35% of the composite at 40-60% of int8 peak) and flags that as the number most likely to be wrong. Metric unchanged at 0.2664.

asi.central_estimate_for_the_kernel_work: both encoders are already on the fastest arithmetic the A78 offers - int8 SDOT, ~4x the fp32 FMA rate, reached because every quantised ggml type declares vec_dot_q8_0 - and they achieve 13-20% of it. The x-asr leg is the weaker half: 12.4 M useful MACs per emitted frame, and because a 61-row window emits only 12 frames its real work is ~5x that, giving ~12.7 G MAC/s against the diar's ~20. Both land at ~4.9 ms per encoder frame, which is a coincidence of model size rather than a shared bottleneck - but it means a kernel win applies to both legs almost equally.

asi.the_most_actionable_item_is_not_the_gemm: the brief's first recommendation is deliberately not the rewrite. ggml re-quantises activations to Q8_0 on EVERY mul_mat call, while a transformer block feeds the same activation tensor to three or four matmuls (q/k/v, the FFN's two projections, attention output). Quantising once per tensor per step instead of once per use is bit-identical - the quantised values are the same, only computed once - and it is a scheduling win inside the existing kernels rather than a new kernel. It is also small enough to measure in a single iteration, which is how it should be tried before committing to a GEMM rewrite that needs kernels this machine does not have.
asi.what_the_brief_says_and_where_the_uncert: docs/kernel-brief.md specifies the work with the numbers a kernel author needs: shapes (x-asr 19 layers, dims 192/256/512/768/512/256, ffn 512/768/1536/2048/1536/768, q5_0; diar 31 layers, hidden 512, ffn 2048, 98.2 M q5_0 weights), the three mechanisms in order of value, and what 'done' looks like. The ceiling is stated as 25-35% of the composite if the encoders reach 40-60% of int8 peak - and flagged as the number MOST LIKELY TO BE WRONG, because it extrapolates from arithmetic intensity and measured efficiency rather than from a prototype. A kernel reaching only 30% of peak would give half of it.
asi.why_a_brief_and_not_a_patch: KleidiAI cannot be built here (the glue is vendored in both ggml copies; no ai_micro_kernels exists anywhere on the machine), so the rewrite cannot be written, tested, or measured in this environment. What CAN be prepared is the part that does not depend on the missing kernels: the measured target, the ordered hypotheses, the bit-identical first attempt, and the measurement discipline needed to tell whether any of it worked. The brief also records a prerequisite - XASR_PROF is racy (one shared unordered_map touched by both worker threads, ~2x inflation) and cannot be used to decide whether a kernel helped, so it must be fixed before it is trusted with that question.

description: Tested the kernel brief's own first recommendation - memoise activation quantisation, bit-identical and needing no new kernel - and measured it instead of building it. Added g_ggml_quant_elems to ggml (counted once per mul_mat call from thread 0, behind GGML_COUNT_QUANT) and had x-asr's profiler print it: the leg quantises 180.8 M activation elements per 69 s clip. But each quantised element contributes one MAC per OUTPUT ROW, so with n_out in 512-2048 it is reused about a thousand times inside the dot: the conversion is ~1/1000 of the arithmetic, ~56 ms per clip, 0.7% of the ASR leg - below the noise band. The mechanism is real, the prize is not, and the brief now drops it. The counter also reconciled an apparent 100x contradiction between two numbers I had recorded separately (12.4 M MACs per frame vs 180 M quantised elements per clip): the ratio is the average output rows per activation element. Metric unchanged at 0.2670.

asi.cost_of_doing_it_wrong: five quiet no-ops this session, and this row produced the worst one: a commit message that described work which was not in the tree. The first edit's python script raised on a LATER anchor before writing the file, so the counter's declaration never persisted while the message claimed it did; the build then failed with 'undeclared identifier' and the deps guard refused to let a stale binary be measured. Every failure was caught downstream rather than at the edit, which is the argument for asserting on edits rather than assuming they applied. Two off-by-one/whitespace mismatches also cost time; the pattern is that matching large code blocks by exact text is fragile, and line-indexed insertion plus a compile check is not.

That looks substantial until you divide by what each element is worth: a quantised activation contributes one MAC per OUTPUT ROW, so with n_out in 512-2048 each element is reused roughly a thousand times inside the dot. The conversion is ~1/1000 of the arithmetic - about 56 ms per clip at 1-2 cycles/element across two threads, i.e. 0.7% of the ASR leg, which is inside the run-to-run band. So the brief's mechanism 1 is real but not worth building, and the brief now says exactly that instead of recommending it.
asi.what_the_counter_reconciled: it also settled a discrepancy I had been carrying without noticing: '12.4 M MACs per emitted frame' and '180 M quantised elements per clip' looked like a 100x contradiction. The ratio is simply the average number of output rows per activation element. Two numbers I had each recorded as facts were consistent all along; what was missing was the quantity that connects them, and building the instrument to measure one thing is what produced it.

description: Closed the kernel brief's own prerequisite and then used it to answer the question the brief had said was inferable. XASR_PROF was a data race - one shared accumulator mutated by both worker threads - so it could not be trusted to judge whether a kernel helped; each thread now owns a thread_local accumulator and dump() merges them under a lock taken only at print time. Added a MUL_MAT histogram by (k x n). The result: essentially ALL of the x-asr encoder's matmul time is in calls with n = 3-24 columns (512x6, 768x3, 1536x3, 256x12 are the top shapes), because the encoder downsamples time by [1,2,4,8,4,2] and a 24-frame chunk reaches the deep, wide stages as 3 columns. At n=3 a GEMM cannot exceed single-digit percent of peak regardless of kernel quality, so the 13-20% figure I had been quoting was a SHAPE result, not a kernel-quality result. Batching - the standard remedy - is unavailable because the column count is the model's streaming chunk. Metric unchanged at 0.2662.

asi.prerequisite_closed: the kernel brief listed 'fix the profiler' as a precondition for trusting any kernel measurement, and it was genuinely broken: the eval callback runs on both worker threads and every field of one shared accumulator was mutated without a lock. It had found real problems (the per-element division) but could not have been trusted to decide whether a new kernel helped. Each thread now owns a thread_local accumulator and dump() merges under a short lock at print time - a mutex per node would serialise the thing being measured.

asi.the_measurement: with the profiler race fixed and a MUL_MAT histogram added, the x-asr encoder's matmul time is almost entirely in calls with n between 3 and 24 columns: 512x6 (9344 calls, 166 us each, 7.9% of accounted), 768x3 (5840, 230 us, 6.9%), 1536x3 (2190, 303 us, 3.4%), 256x12 (4672, 101 us, 2.4%), 1152x6 (2336, 187 us, 2.2%); the top 12 of 54 distinct shapes cover about a third of accounted time. The cause is structural - the encoder downsamples time by [1,2,4,8,4,2] across six stages, so a 24-frame chunk reaches the deep, wide stages (dims 512-768, ffn 1536-2048, where most parameters live) as 3 columns.
asi.why_this_closes_the_diagnosis: at n=3 a GEMM reaches single-digit percent of int8 peak no matter how good the kernel is: there is no reuse of the weight matrix across columns to amortise the stream, and per-call setup plus the thread barrier dominate. So the '13-20% of peak' I had been quoting was never a kernel-quality figure - it was a shape figure, and the two call for completely different responses. Batching skinny GEMMs is the standard remedy and it is UNAVAILABLE here, because the column count is the time axis after downsampling and the model's streaming chunk fixes it; enlarging the chunk is the change already measured at +5.9 WER on the primary gate clip, and halving the step count while keeping the same rows would recompute rows the model already emitted. The shape therefore cannot be engineered away in-graph.
asi.what_the_brief_says_now: the requirement is sharper and narrower than 'make the GEMM faster': a kernel that is fast at n = 3-24 with k in 192-2560, int8 accumulate into int32, two threads on two A78s. A kernel tuned for large N would not help this workload at all - which is also the most useful thing to tell someone about to spend time on KleidiAI, since the temptation will be to benchmark it on large square matmuls where it looks excellent.

description: Completed the shape analysis on the other leg, and it inverts the priority. The diar encoder's MUL_MAT shapes are k = 512/1536/2048 with n = 351, 380, 548 - conventional GEMM shapes with hundreds of columns - the opposite of the ASR's n = 3-24. That also explains the measured efficiency gap between the legs (diar ~20 G MAC/s vs x-asr ~12.7) with no appeal to kernel quality: same library, same instructions, same weight format, different shapes. So the best remaining target is the diar: about a quarter of the composite, already feeding kernels the shape they handle well, and the leg this project has spent the least time on. The ASR's small-N problem remains a separate, harder project whose usual remedy (batching) is unavailable because the column count is the model's streaming chunk. Metric unchanged at 0.2674.

Hundreds of columns, exactly the regime a tuned int8 GEMM is built for. asi.why_it_matters_more_than_the_number: it inverts the priority. A 2-3x on the diar encoder is plausible with a drop-in GEMM replacement and has no structural obstacle. The ASR's small-N problem is a separate, harder project whose usual remedy is unavailable.
asi.what_a_resumer_should_do: diar first, ASR second - and do NOT validate a candidate GEMM on large square matmuls, which is what everyone does and which would show the diar case beautifully and the ASR case not at all. For the diar the requirement is unremarkable (k in {512, 1536, 2048}, n in {351, 548}, int8 accumulate to int32, f32 out, two threads on two A78s). The availability question is the same for both: KleidiAI's kernels are not on this machine, so the work is a specification until someone fetches them.

description: Proposed converting the diar's weights from q5_0 to q8_0 so its matmuls would reach ggml's .nrows = 2 dotprod path, with a sharp prediction from the shape analysis (helps the diar at 351-548 columns, does nothing for the ASR at n = 3-24, which also explains the early format sweep tying). Built the converter, and it failed - and the failure exposed that BOTH models already ship Q8_0. These ggml copies number types Q5_0=6, Q8_0=8; the histograms were read with the older llama.cpp numbering where 8 means q5_0. Confirmed twice independently: payload density is 8.5 bits/element (q8_0, not q5_0's 5.5), and gguf_get_tensor_size disagreed with my q5_0 arithmetic. So the hypothesis was dead on arrival, and the correction matters more than the speed run.

asi.how_it_was_caught_and_what_it_cost: the clue arrived as a parser failure: my q5_0 -> q8_0 converter could not reshape a 278,528-byte payload into 22-byte blocks, and gguf_get_tensor_size returned the same 278,528 where q5_0 arithmetic expected 180,224. I spent several steps treating that as an offset bug in MY code before dividing 278,528 by 512x512 and getting 1.0625 bytes/element - 8.5 bits, which is q8_0's density and not q5_0's 5.5. Two independent facts were sitting in front of me and the one I trusted was my own arithmetic. The lesson is narrow and checkable: when a library and your arithmetic disagree about a file format, ask the library - which is now gsize.c in the session, and takes seconds.
asi.hypothesis: ggml gives Q8_0 .nrows = 2 under dotprod (two weight rows per activation load) but hard-codes Q5_0 to .nrows = 1, and the diar ships q5_0 - so converting the diar to q8_0 should roughly halve its activation traffic. The shape analysis says the diar runs 351-548 columns, where activation traffic dominates, unlike the ASR's n = 3-24 where it does not - which also explains why the early ASR format sweep tied.

asi.what_dies_and_what_survives: Dead: 'the diar's weights are q5_0', 'the diar is missing the two-row path', and any conversion motivated by either - tools/requant_gguf.py is deleted rather than left looking plausible. Alive and reinforced: weight format cannot help this composite, because every quantised type dots through vec_dot_q8_0 and int8 SDOT is the core's fastest arithmetic, and the shipped weights are already the type that gets .nrows = 2. The conclusion was right and the reasoning was wrong, which is worth recording on its own: a right answer for the wrong reason does not survive the next person who reads the evidence. Also noted: the requantisation sweep's 'all q8_0' arm was probably vacuous for the same reason, though q4_k / q4_0 / iq4_nl / q6_k were genuine conversions, so the sweep's conclusion stands. Unaffected: every shape and timing measurement in the brief, which came from the profilers rather than from dtype histograms.

asi.row_meaning: this row changes no measured code. It closes the loop on the previous row's error by making the CLASS of error detectable rather than just correcting the instance - which matters because that error supported several conclusions in the ledger, and because the next person to read a GGUF here will hit the same enum trap.
asi.the_general_fix_is_a_self_checking_numbe: the enum mistake was not fixed by memorising a different enum - enums are exactly the thing you get wrong from memory. The fix is to report a quantity that cannot be mislabelled: bits per element, derived from payload size and element count with no enum involved. A tensor called q5_0 occupying 8.5 bits per element is visibly not a q5_0. Cross-checked against gguf_get_tensor_size, the table validates itself, and both halves cost seconds.
asi.what_this_buys_the_next_iteration: every remaining claim in the brief now rests on numbers that carry their own verification: shapes and times from the profilers, density-checked dtypes from the inventory, and the gate's byte-identity on the transcripts themselves. If a future candidate changes a weight format - the one lever that is closed by arithmetic - the first question is answered by running one command rather than by re-deriving an enum from memory.

description: Stopped splitting skinny matmuls across threads: the x-asr encoder runs its GEMMs at 3-24 columns and issues ~65k per 69 s clip, so each call was paying a two-thread dispatch and a barrier to hand one or two columns to the second core. Below 16 columns the rows now stay on one thread - bit-identical, since row partitioning decides which core runs a row and not what is computed. Measured flat: 0.2667 vs 0.2666, asr_s 37.96 vs 38.00, gate byte-identical. Kept because it is strictly less synchronisation and demonstrably not harmful, not because it is faster.

asi.change: ref/crispasr/ggml 512a020: ggml_get_n_tasks now sends MUL_MAT to one thread below 16 columns. Row partitioning is untouched, so this is bit-identical, and the host gate confirms it (hash 192184ebcd54977e, WER and attribution unchanged).
asi.confounded_reading_i_had_to_discard: I compared cores_used 0.98 before and 1.74 after and it looked like a clean win - then noticed the 'before' was an ASR-only probe from EARLY in the session, before graph reuse, the f16 joint and buffer reuse. The wall time in that same probe was 25.0 s for chat69 and is 11.5 s now, which is the sum of all those changes, not this one. So the utilisation difference is not attributable to this commit, and I am not claiming it. The barrier tax remains a plausible mechanism with no measured effect.
asi.hypothesis: the x-asr encoder runs its GEMMs at 3-24 columns and issues ~65k of them per 69 s clip, so every call paid a two-thread dispatch and a barrier to hand one or two columns to the second core; keeping skinny matmuls on one thread should remove that tax
asi.kept_because_it_is_strictly_less_work_no: bit-identical (row partitioning decides which core runs a row, not what is computed), strictly fewer synchronisations, and measured neutral rather than harmful - the same standard applied to the earlier copy/elementwise threshold. Had it shown a regression I would have reverted it.

asi.next: the remaining open question on this axis is whether the ASR leg is limited by the barrier between ops or by op-level parallelism being unavailable at n=3-24. The composite now reports 1.82 of 2 cores, so there is little headroom left in utilisation - which means the ASR's 9.5 s per clip is close to what two A78s can do on 3-column GEMMs, and the only remaining lever is a kernel that makes those shapes fundamentally cheaper rather than better scheduled. That is the same conclusion the shape analysis reached, now with a utilisation number attached.
asi.session_pattern: this is the sixth and final member of a family: an idea that sounded mechanically sound, cost an hour to build, and measured 0%. Copy removal, thread-partition threshold, per-element division, buffer reuse, activation-quantisation memoisation, and now skinny-matmul scheduling. In every case the change was bit-identical and strictly less work, and in every case the wall clock did not move - because the ASR leg is limited by the arithmetic in 3-column GEMMs, not by how that arithmetic is scheduled. The pattern is itself the finding, and it is why the kernel brief now points at the shapes rather than at the plumbing.
